passages.t: Write it in a book: the time of Jacob's distress
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah, ‘Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you’ (verse 2). The days are coming when he will bring Israel and Judah back from captivity to the land he gave their fathers (verse 3).

A cry of panic is heard, terror and not peace (verse 5). Can a man give birth? Then why does every man hold his stomach like a woman in labor, his face turned pale (verse 6)? “How awful that day will be! None will be like it! It is the time of Jacob’s distress, but he will be saved out of it” (verse 7).

On that day God will break the yoke off their necks, and strangers will no longer enslave them (verse 8). ‘Instead, they will serve the LORD their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them’ (verse 9). Jacob, God's servant, is not to be afraid, for God will save him from far away and bring his children back from exile, and Jacob will have rest (verse 10). God will make a full end of the nations where he scattered them, but not of Jacob. He will discipline him justly and not leave him unpunished (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 30 to 33 are often called the Book of Consolation. They are not dated one by one. Chapter 32 places Jeremiah's purchase of a field in the tenth year of Zedekiah, about 588 or 587 BC, while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and many scholars think the collection took shape around then. Some poems may come from Jeremiah's earlier words to the northern tribes.

The command to write is important. The comfort was for a later generation, so it had to be kept on a scroll until it was needed.

Men clutching their stomachs like women in labor is a picture of terror so great it doubles a strong man over. The day of distress is real. But it ends with the words he will be saved out of it.

David their king, whom God will raise up, does not mean David rising from the dead. It means a king of David's line, the promised ruler.
passages.later: Daniel speaks of a coming ‘time of distress’ (Daniel 12:1), and Hosea says Israel will ‘seek the LORD their God and David their king’ (Hosea 3:5). Ezekiel promises, ‘My servant David will be king over them’ (Ezekiel 37:24).
passages.hard:
What is the time of Jacob's distress, and is it about the end times?

Readers take verse 7 in different ways. Many interpreters, especially in the dispensational tradition, read it as a prophecy of a future time of great tribulation for the Jewish people at the end of the age, followed by national deliverance, joining it with Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:21. Others read it in its own setting as the Babylonian conquest and exile, a day without equal for Judah, from which the nation was saved by the return under Persia; the surrounding verses speak of breaking Babylon's yoke and coming home. Still others see a pattern in which a historical judgment and rescue foreshadow a final one.

All agree on the chapter's main point: God's people pass through a day of real anguish, and he brings them out. The details of future events are a second-order question on which faithful readers differ. These notes set no date and identify no event of the present day with this verse.
passages.asks: The day of distress ends with the words he will be saved out of it. Ask what distress you are in, and whether you can hold on to the end of that sentence. And ask why God would have these words written down for people who did not yet need them.

passages.t: An incurable wound, and God will heal
passages.happening:
‘Your injury is incurable; your wound is grievous’ (verse 12). No one pleads Zion's cause; there is no remedy (verse 13). All her lovers have forgotten her, for God struck her as an enemy would, because of her great guilt (verse 14). Why cry out over the wound? It has no cure (verse 15).

‘Nevertheless, all who devour you will be devoured’ (verse 16). ‘But I will restore your health and heal your wounds, declares the LORD, because they call you an outcast, Zion, for whom no one cares’ (verse 17).

God will restore Jacob's tents, and the city will be rebuilt on its mound and the palace stand in its place (verse 18). Thanksgiving and celebration will come from them, and God will multiply and honor them (verse 19). ‘Their leader will be one of their own, and their ruler will arise from their midst’ (verse 21). God will bring him near, and he will approach God, for who would dare do so on his own (verse 21)? ‘And you will be My people, and I will be your God’ (verse 22).

The storm of the LORD goes out against the wicked, and his anger will not turn back until he has done all he intends. In the days to come they will understand (verses 23 and 24).
passages.hearers:
The lovers of verse 14 are Judah's former allies, above all Egypt, on whom its kings had relied against Babylon. They forgot Zion when she fell.

The wound is called incurable, and then God says he will heal it. Both are true. No human remedy could heal Judah. Only God could.

Outcast, a city no one cares for, is what the nations called Zion. God answers that taunt by caring for her himself.

The city rebuilt on its mound is the tell, the mound built up by generations of settlement, on which ancient towns were rebuilt. A ruler who approaches God was a priestly picture: only someone God brought near could come close without dying.
passages.later: Hosea uses the same words of covenant: ‘You are My people’ (Hosea 2:23). The psalmist says, ‘He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds’ (Psalm 147:3).
passages.asks: God calls the wound incurable and then promises to heal it. Ask what in you no human remedy can reach. And ask what it would mean for you to be cared for by God when others have called you an outcast.
